sections.title: Mental model — std::sort is a committee

blocks.md: Interviewers ask "how does std::sort work?" expecting the three-act story: **introsort** starts as randomized quicksort; if recursion depth breaches ≈2·log₂n it suspects adversarial input and switches that subrange to HEAPSORT (guaranteed n log n); finally a pass of INSERTION SORT polishes nearly-sorted small runs (cache-friendly, low overhead). Name all three acts = instant credibility.

steps: Act 2: depth > 2·log₂n? → heapsort that region (worst-case insurance)
Act 3: final insertion-sort sweep over tiny runs (fast on almost-sorted)
Result: Θ(n log n) worst case + practical speed

chain.q: Why insertion for small runs instead of just recursing?
chain.a: Function-call overhead + partition constants dominate at n≤~16; insertion's tight loop wins there. Same reason Timsort/minrun exists in Python/Java.

chain.q: When would you pick stable_sort deliberately?
chain.a: Multi-key sorting via repeated stable passes (sort by secondary key THEN primary) — stability carries earlier order through. Classic: sort names by dept then salary with two stable sorts instead of fat comparator.

chain.q: Heapsort vs merge sort both n log n — why does introsort pick heapsort as bodyguard?
chain.a: In-place O(1) auxiliary vs merge's O(n) buffer; insurance shouldn't cost memory. Downside (poor cache locality) irrelevant since it rarely triggers.

items.q: Multi-key sort via two stable passes: which key sorted FIRST?
items.explain: Later pass takes precedence; earlier survives within ties.

options: make n² impossible while allowing normal random depth ~log n headroom
items.explain: Normal quicksort never approaches it; killers get caught.

blocks.md: **Scale question template:** chunk what fits → sort each chunk → merge streams. 'Sort 10GB in 1GB RAM' = external mergesort; say 'priority queue drives the k-way merge' and watch interviewer nod.

chain.q: Sort 10 GB of 100-byte records, 1 GB RAM?
chain.a: Read 1 GB chunks → in-memory introsort each → write runs. Then 10-way merge with buffered readers + min-heap of run-heads (record, runId). Complexity Θ(N log N) I/O-amortized; mention multiway fan-in tuning.

chain.q: Why is mergesort preferred for linked lists but quicksort for arrays?
chain.a: Lists: no random access hurts quicksort scans, merge needs only pointer splicing + Θ(log n) stack. Arrays: quicksort's in-place cache-friendly partition beats paying Θ(n) buffer.

chain.q: Comparator throwing or violating strict ordering inside sort?
chain.a: UB — libstdc++ descends out-of-bounds (the famous segfault). Always fuzz comparators with duplicate-heavy tests; recall strict-weak-ordering rules from Foundations L4.

options: I/O transfers — hence buffering & fan-in design
items.explain: Disk/network latency dominates; algorithmic work secondary.

options: detects natural sorted RUNS and merges them — near-linear on real data
items.explain: Run detection + minrun galloping exploits partial order; worst case stays Θ(n log n).

items.title: First Missing Positive
items.statement: Smallest missing positive in O(n)/O(1). Values-as-indices is THE idea.
hints: Cycle-sort values into 1..n homes, ignore others.
Scan: first a[i]≠i+1 answers i+1; else n+1.
Defend linearity: each swap places one element permanently.

solutionCode.label: cyclic sort: send value v to index v-1

items.complexity: Time O(n) — each swap parks one value permanently, so total swaps ≤ n. Space O(1), the array is its own hash table.

followups.q: Defend the linearity despite the nested while loop.
followups.a: Every iteration of the while loop places some value into its correct home, and a value in its home is never moved again. There are at most n values that can ever be homed, so the while loop bodies execute at most n times across the whole outer loop — O(n) total, not O(n²).

followups.q: Why is the guard `a[a[i]-1] != a[i]` rather than `a[i] != i+1`?
followups.a: It is the duplicate protection. With input [1,1], the second 1 wants index 0, which already holds a 1 — swapping would loop forever. Comparing against the *destination* value stops as soon as the home is already occupied by an equal value.

items.title: Sort List (linked list)
items.statement: O(n log n) sort of singly list; then eliminate recursion via bottom-up merging.
hints: Top-down classic first; bottom-up = widths 1,2,4… splicing runs.
Bonus sentence: why quicksort dies here (no random access).

solutionCode.label: top-down split via slow/fast, then bottom-up to kill recursion

items.complexity: O(n log n) time. Top-down uses O(log n) recursion stack; bottom-up is O(1) auxiliary space.

followups.q: Why does quicksort die on a linked list?
followups.a: Partitioning needs to walk inward from both ends, which requires random access or a backward pointer — a singly-linked list has neither. You can only move forward, so choosing a pivot and partitioning costs extra passes, and the O(n²) worst case has no cheap randomisation defence. Merge sort only ever needs sequential access, which is exactly what a list offers.

followups.q: What does the bottom-up version buy?
followups.a: It removes the O(log n) recursion stack, giving genuine O(1) auxiliary space. You merge runs of width 1, then 2, then 4, splicing them back into one list each pass. The trade is fiddlier pointer bookkeeping — worth it only when the interviewer explicitly asks for constant space.

items.title: Maximum Gap
items.statement: Max adjacent difference after sorting — linear WITHOUT actually sorting.
hints: Track per-bucket min/max; answer = max(minB − prevMaxB).
Prove gap can't live INSIDE a bucket.

solutionCode.label: pigeonhole buckets; the answer can only cross a bucket boundary
solutionCode.py:
import math


def maximum_gap(a: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(a)
    if n < 2:
        return 0
    lo, hi = min(a), max(a)
    if lo == hi:
        return 0

    # n-1 buckets over the range => average gap <= bucket width
    width = max(1, math.ceil((hi - lo) / (n - 1)))
    count = (hi - lo) // width + 1
    bmin = [None] * count
    bmax = [None] * count
    for x in a:
        b = (x - lo) // width
        bmin[b] = x if bmin[b] is None else min(bmin[b], x)
        bmax[b] = x if bmax[b] is None else max(bmax[b], x)

    best, prev_max = 0, lo
    for b in range(count):
        if bmin[b] is None:
            continue                       # empty bucket: skip
        best = max(best, bmin[b] - prev_max)   # gap spans the empty run
        prev_max = bmax[b]
    return best

items.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space — buckets are filled in one pass and scanned in one pass. No comparison sort involved.

followups.q: Prove the maximum gap cannot lie inside a bucket.
followups.a: With n elements spread over range (hi−lo), the average adjacent gap is (hi−lo)/(n−1), so the maximum gap is at least that. Bucket width is set to exactly that value, so any two elements inside one bucket differ by less than the average gap — strictly less than the maximum. The answer must therefore span a boundary, which is why only per-bucket min and max matter.

followups.q: Why n−1 buckets rather than n?
followups.a: There are n−1 adjacent gaps among n sorted elements. Sizing the buckets to that count makes the width equal the average gap, which is what licenses the argument above. With n buckets the width shrinks and the pigeonhole guarantee — at least one empty bucket — is lost.

items.title: Wiggle Sort II
items.statement: Strict wiggle with duplicates allowed. Show naive failure, then nth_element + virtual index solution.
hints: Virtual map: idx(1,3,5…) vs reversed placement keeps equals apart.
Explain coloring pass on virtual order.

solutionCode.label: median split, then interleave larger-half into odd slots

items.complexity: O(n) average with nth_element for the median, then one O(n) placement pass. Space O(n) for the output here; an in-place virtual-index version is O(1).

followups.q: Show why the naive "split and interleave forwards" fails.
followups.a: Take [1,1,2,2]. Halves are [1,1] and [2,2]; interleaving forwards gives 1,2,1,2 — fine. But [1,1,1,2,2,2] gives halves [1,1,1] and [2,2,2] and forward interleave yields 1,2,1,2,1,2 which works, while [4,5,5,6] gives [4,5],[5,6] → 4,5,5,6: the two 5s become adjacent and the strict wiggle fails. Reading each half from its largest end pushes duplicates to opposite ends of the output.

followups.q: Why does descending traversal separate equal values?
followups.a: Duplicates cluster around the median, i.e. at the *end* of the smaller half and the *start* of the larger half. Consuming both halves from their high ends places those neighbours at maximum index distance in the output, so they can never land in adjacent slots.

followups.q: When does no valid answer exist at all?
followups.a: A count-based rule of thumb ("no value more than ceil(n/2) times") is necessary but NOT sufficient. [1,2,2,2,3] has three 2s with n = 5, satisfies that bound, and still admits no strict wiggle: all three 2s must take the three valley slots, leaving 1 and 3 as peaks, and the peak holding 1 cannot exceed its neighbours. LeetCode 324 guarantees the input is solvable — say so rather than pretending the algorithm validates its own input.

items.title: Pancake Sorting (generalized)
items.statement: Return flip sequence sorting any array within 2n flips; prove bound.
hints: Shrink n each pair; induction finishes proof.

solutionCode.label: two flips per element, proved by induction on the shrinking prefix

items.complexity: At most 2(n−1) flips; each flip is O(n), so O(n²) work. Space O(1) beyond the flip list.

followups.q: Give the induction proving the 2n bound.
followups.a: Claim: sorting a prefix of length k costs at most 2(k−1) flips. Base case k = 1 is trivially 0. For k, two flips park the maximum at position k−1 permanently, leaving a prefix of length k−1 which by hypothesis costs at most 2(k−2). Total 2 + 2(k−2) = 2(k−1). So n elements cost at most 2(n−1) < 2n.

followups.q: Where does the bound become loose?
followups.a: Whenever the maximum is already at the end of the unsorted prefix, that round costs zero flips instead of two — so a nearly-sorted array does far better than 2n. The bound is worst-case, not typical. The known optimal bound for pancake sorting is roughly 1.64n, but achieving it is a research-level result, not an interview answer.

items.title: External Sort Simulator
items.statement: Simulate sorting 100MB with 10MB RAM: write chunk files, then merge with heap of stream heads. Report I/O passes.
hints: Heap entries (headValue, runIdx); pop-push cycle per output.
Discuss fan-in increase to cut passes.

solutionCode.label: chunk-sort into runs, then k-way merge with a heap of run heads
solutionCode.py:
import heapq


class ExternalSort:
    """Simulates external sort: data too large for RAM is split into sorted
    runs, then merged with a heap holding one element per run."""

    def __init__(self, chunk_size: int):
        self.chunk_size = chunk_size
        self.runs = []              # stand-ins for on-disk files
        self.read_ops = 0
        self.write_ops = 0

    def make_runs(self, data: list[int]) -> None:
        """PASS 1: read a chunk, sort it in RAM, spill it as a sorted run."""
        for i in range(0, len(data), self.chunk_size):
            run = data[i:i + self.chunk_size]
            self.read_ops += len(run)
            run.sort()
            self.write_ops += len(run)
            self.runs.append(run)

    def merge_runs(self) -> list[int]:
        """PASS 2: heap of (value, run_idx, offset); pop smallest, push next."""
        pq = [(run[0], r, 0) for r, run in enumerate(self.runs) if run]
        heapq.heapify(pq)
        out = []
        while pq:
            val, r, off = heapq.heappop(pq)
            out.append(val)
            self.read_ops += 1
            self.write_ops += 1
            if off + 1 < len(self.runs[r]):
                heapq.heappush(pq, (self.runs[r][off + 1], r, off + 1))
        return out

    def passes(self) -> int:
        return 2 if self.runs else 0

items.complexity: Two I/O passes: one to write sorted runs, one to merge them. Time O(N log N) total; memory bounded by the chunk size plus the k-entry heap.

followups.q: 100 MB of data with 10 MB of RAM — what happens?
followups.a: Pass 1 produces 10 sorted runs of 10 MB each, reading and writing 100 MB. Pass 2 merges all 10 at once with a 10-entry heap, reading and writing 100 MB again. Two passes, 200 MB of I/O each way. The heap holds only one record per run, so RAM stays bounded regardless of total size.

followups.q: How does increasing fan-in cut passes?
followups.a: If the number of runs exceeds what one merge can hold open, you need multiple merge rounds — passes grow as log_k(runs) for fan-in k. Raising k merges more runs per pass, so total I/O drops. The limit is memory: each open run needs a buffer, so very large k shrinks each buffer and costs more seeks per byte. The optimum trades pass count against buffer size.
